questions.stem: What does 「卒業式」 mean?
options: An entrance ceremony
An end-of-term ceremony
A school sports day
A graduation ceremony
questions.explanation: 「卒業」 is graduation and 「式」 is a ceremony. An entrance ceremony is 「入学式」, the ceremony at the end of a term is 「終業式」, and sports day is 「運動会」.

questions.stem: In Japan, in which month are school graduation ceremonies usually held?
options: July
March
April
December
questions.explanation: The Japanese school year begins in April and ends in March, so graduation ceremonies fall in March, at the end of the year. April is when entrance ceremonies welcome new students; December is when the Australian school year ends.

questions.stem: 「日本では、四月に入学式があって、三月に卒業式があります。」 What does the sentence tell you about the Japanese school year?
options: It starts in April and finishes in March
It starts in March and finishes in April
It starts in January and finishes in December
It has two graduations, in March and April
questions.explanation: The entrance ceremony (入学式) is in April and the graduation ceremony (卒業式) is in March, so the year runs from April to March. That is why Japanese students graduate in spring, while Queensland Year 12s finish in November.

questions.stem: What is a 「卒業しょうしょ」?
options: The letter of thanks the class writes to its teachers
The certificate given to each graduate
The speech a graduate gives on behalf of the year
The album of class photos given at graduation
questions.explanation: A 卒業しょうしょ is the graduation certificate, which the principal hands to each graduate during the ceremony. The book of class photos is a 「卒業アルバム」.

questions.stem: Who is the 「校長先生」 at a Japanese school?
options: The school captain
The careers adviser
The principal
The homeroom teacher
questions.explanation: 「校長」 is the head of a school, so 校長先生 is the principal, who usually speaks at the graduation ceremony. The homeroom teacher is the 「たんにんの先生」.

questions.stem: What does 「卒業生」 mean?
options: The teachers
The graduates
The new students
The parents
questions.explanation: 「卒業生」 combines 卒業 (graduation) with 「生」 (student), so it means the graduating students or graduates. New students are 「新入生」.

questions.stem: On the last day, a graduate thanks her teachers for three years of care. Which sentence does she use?
options: 「三年間、ほんとうにごちそうさまでした。」
「三年間、ほんとうにお世話になりました。」
「三年間、ほんとうにお世話になります。」
「三年間、ほんとうにお待たせしました。」
questions.explanation: 「お世話になりました」, in the past tense, thanks someone for care already received, which suits a farewell. 「お世話になります」 is said at the start of a stay or a relationship, looking forward rather than back.

questions.stem: 「日本の卒業式は、卒業しょうしょをもらうだけの日ではなく、お世話になった人にかんしゃをつたえる日でもある。」 What significance does the writer give the ceremony?
options: It is mainly a day to celebrate with friends
A day also for thanking those who helped you
It is mainly a day to receive the certificate
It is a day for teachers to thank the students
questions.explanation: 「〜だけの日ではなく、〜日でもある」 means 'not just a day for..., but also a day for...'. The writer adds a second meaning: expressing gratitude (かんしゃ) to those who looked after you. Receiving the certificate is the meaning the writer says is not the whole story.

questions.stem: What is a 「よせがき」?
options: A diary that a class keeps together during the year
The list of graduates read out at the ceremony
A card or board covered in messages from many people
A letter one student writes to the whole school
questions.explanation: A よせがき gathers messages from many people on one card, board or sheet, and is often given at graduations and farewells. The key idea is many writers on one item.

questions.stem: Which message would you most likely write on a よせがき for a friend who is graduating?
options: 「明日のテストは九時から始まります。」
「いらっしゃいませ。何名様ですか。」
「ごみは月曜日の朝に出してください。」
「三年間ありがとう！大学に行ってもがんばってね。」
questions.explanation: A よせがき message thanks the person and wishes them well, often in friendly plain style. The others are a test notice, a restaurant greeting and a rubbish rule.

questions.stem: On graduation day, some boys give the second button of their school jacket to someone special. Why is the second button the one traditionally asked for?
options: It shows which year level the student is in
It is said to sit closest to the heart
It is the button that carries the school badge
It is the easiest button to remove neatly
questions.explanation: The most common explanation is that the second button sits nearest the heart, so receiving it means receiving the boy's heart. The custom is linked to the stand-up collar jacket and is becoming less common as fewer schools use that uniform.

questions.stem: 「卒業式のあと、友達や先生といっしょにしゃしんをとったり、花をもらったりしました。」 What did the writer do after the ceremony?
options: Had dinner with friends and teachers, and bought flowers
Took photos with friends and teachers, and received flowers
Gave flowers to friends and teachers, and took photos of them
Took photos of the flowers that the teachers had brought
questions.explanation: 「〜たり、〜たりしました」 lists examples of things done: taking photos (しゃしんをとる) and receiving flowers (花をもらう). 「もらう」 is to receive, so the writer was given the flowers rather than giving them.

questions.stem: 「学校生活の一番の思い出は、しゅうがく旅行です。」 What is the writer's best memory of school life?
options: The school trip
The graduation ceremony
The school sports day
The club tournament
questions.explanation: 「思い出」 is a memory, and 「しゅうがく旅行」 is the school trip many Japanese students take together. Sports day would be 「運動会」.

questions.stem: 「三年生は夏の大会のあと部活をいんたいして、受験勉強を始めます。」 What does the sentence say?
options: After the summer tournament, third-years leave their clubs and start exam study
After the summer holidays, third-years join new clubs and start a tournament
Third-years study for exams during the summer tournament and then rejoin clubs
Before the summer tournament, third-years stop studying to train with their clubs
questions.explanation: 「いんたいする」 is to retire, here from club activities (部活), and 「受験勉強」 is study for entrance exams. The order is set by 「〜のあと」: after the summer tournament.

questions.stem: What does 「受験」 mean?
options: Sitting entrance exams
Graduating from school
Choosing a university course
Starting a new job
questions.explanation: 「受ける」 is to take and 「験」 comes from 「試験」 (exam), so 受験 is sitting an exam, usually an entrance exam for a high school or university. Graduating is 「卒業」.

questions.stem: 「クイーンズランドでは、十二年生が卒業したあと、友達とゴールドコーストなどに行って、一週間ぐらい楽しむ『スクーリーズ』があります。」 What does the passage describe?
options: A school trip that teachers organise for all of Year 12
A week of celebration with friends after Year 12 finishes
A graduation ceremony held at the beach for Year 12
A week of exams that Year 12 students sit before graduating
questions.explanation: The passage says that after Year 12 graduate (卒業したあと) they go with friends to places such as the Gold Coast and enjoy about a week (一週間ぐらい). Nothing says the school organises it or that it is a ceremony.

questions.stem: A Japanese exchange student writes: 「日本の卒業式はしずかで、まじめですが、オーストラリアのフォーマルはにぎやかで楽しそうです。」 What contrast does she draw?
options: A lively, fun ceremony against a formal that looks quiet and serious
A quiet, serious ceremony against a formal she found lively and fun
A ceremony that is quieter and more serious than the one she had expected
A quiet, serious ceremony against a formal that looks lively and fun
questions.explanation: 「しずかで、まじめ」 describes the Japanese ceremony, and 「にぎやかで楽しそう」 the formal. 「楽しそう」 is appearance: it looks fun, a judgement from outside, so she is not reporting her own night at a formal.

questions.stem: 「オーストラリアでは、十二年生の最後の日に、友達どうしでシャツにサインをしあうことがあります。日本のよせがきに少しにています。」 What comparison is made?
options: Friends signing each other's shirts is quite unlike a よせがき
Students wear their よせがき shirt to the graduation ceremony
Japanese students sign shirts instead of writing a よせがき
Friends signing each other's shirts is a little like a よせがき
questions.explanation: 「〜にています」 means 'resembles', and 「少し」 softens it to 'a little like'. Both customs collect messages or names from many friends on one item at the end of school.

questions.stem: At the graduation, a teacher says 「卒業生のご家族も、たくさんいらっしゃいました。」 What does 「いらっしゃいました」 mean here?
options: were waiting (humble)
went home (respectful)
were invited (humble)
came (respectful)
questions.explanation: 「いらっしゃる」 is the respectful verb for 'come', 'go' or 'be'; here it shows respect to the graduates' families who came. It raises the people being spoken about, so it is respectful rather than humble.

questions.stem: 「三年間は、あっというまに終わってしまいました。」 What does 〜てしまいました add?
options: A wish that the three years would soon be over
Permission for the three years to come to an end
A sense of regret or surprise that the three years are over
A plan to finish the three years earlier than usual
questions.explanation: 「〜てしまう」 marks an action as complete and often adds regret or surprise. With 「あっというまに」 ('in an instant'), the writer is surprised and a little sad that school is already over, not wishing it away.

questions.stem: 「卒業したら、一年間ボランティアをすることにしました。」 What does the speaker say?
options: I have decided to volunteer for a year after I graduate
It has been decided that I will volunteer for a year after graduating
I am wondering whether to volunteer for a year after I graduate
I have already volunteered for a year since I graduated
questions.explanation: 「〜ことにする」 states the speaker's own decision, so 「することにしました」 is 'I have decided to do'. A decision made by others or by circumstance would be 「〜ことになりました」.

questions.stem: 「先生には、いつまでも元気でいてほしいです。」 What does the writer say?
options: I want my teacher to stay well always
I want to stay as well as my teacher
My teacher wants us to stay well always
I hope I can always visit my teacher
questions.explanation: 「〜てほしい」 expresses wanting someone else to do or be something, and the person is marked with 「に」 (here 「先生には」). So the wish is for the teacher to stay healthy (元気でいる).

questions.stem: 「卒業しても、ずっと友達でいようね。」 What does the speaker say?
options: Before we graduate, let's become close friends
Even after we graduate, let's always stay friends
Once we graduate, we will not be friends any more
If we graduate together, let's become friends
questions.explanation: 「〜ても」 means 'even if' or 'even after', and 「いよう」 is the volitional of 「いる」, 'let's be'. So the friendship is to continue in spite of graduation.

questions.stem: 「今、卒業式が終わったところです。」 What does the sentence mean?
options: The graduation ceremony has just finished
The graduation ceremony is about to finish
The graduation ceremony is still going on
The graduation ceremony finished long ago
questions.explanation: Past tense + 「ところ」 means something has just happened. 'About to finish' would be 「終わるところ」 and 'still going on' 「しているところ」.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「卒業式で ___ ように、毎日スピーチのれんしゅうをしています。」 ('I practise my speech every day so that I won't cry at the ceremony')?
options: なかなくて
なかないで
ないた
なかない
questions.explanation: 「ように」 for a purpose or hoped-for result follows the plain form, here the plain negative 「なかない」: 'so that I won't cry'. 「なかないで」 is a request or 'without crying', and 「ないた」 is past, which does not fit a goal.

questions.stem: 「大学に入っても、毎日日本語を話すようにします。」 What does the speaker say?
options: I was told to speak Japanese every day
I will speak Japanese the way Japanese people do
I will make a point of speaking Japanese every day
I have become able to speak Japanese every day
questions.explanation: 「〜ようにする」 means to make an effort to do something regularly. 「〜ようになる」 would describe a change in ability ('have come to be able to'), and 'told to' would be 「〜ように言われる」.

questions.stem: What does 「ボランティア活動」 mean?
options: Job hunting
Volunteer work
Part-time work
Club activities
questions.explanation: 「活動」 is activity, so ボランティア活動 is volunteer work. Part-time work is 「アルバイト」, club activities are 「部活」 and job hunting is 「しゅうかつ」.

questions.stem: What does 「町のごみひろいにさんかしました。」 mean?
options: I complained about the litter in my town
I sorted the rubbish at the town hall
I took part in a litter clean-up in my town
I organised the rubbish collection in my town
questions.explanation: 「ごみひろい」 is picking up litter and 「さんかする」 is to take part, with the event marked by 「に」. The speaker joined the clean-up rather than organising it.

questions.stem: Why is 1995 often called Japan's 「ボランティア元年」?
options: Volunteering became a required subject in Japanese schools that year
Tokyo recruited thousands of volunteers for the Olympic Games that year
Huge numbers volunteered after the Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake
Japan passed its first law setting up volunteer groups that year
questions.explanation: 「元年」 means the first year of something. After the earthquake of January 1995, well over a million volunteers went to help within the first year, the first turnout on that scale in Japan. Laws for non-profit groups came later, in 1998.

questions.stem: 「ボランティアをすると、いろいろな人と知りあえるし、自分にじしんもつきます。」 What benefits does the writer give?
options: Earning some money and gaining work experience
Making the community cleaner and safer to live in
Learning new skills and adding to a job application
Meeting many kinds of people and gaining confidence
questions.explanation: 「知りあえる」 is the potential of 「知りあう」, being able to get to know people, and 「じしんがつく」 is to gain confidence. The 「し」 links the two reasons. Money and job applications are not mentioned.

questions.stem: 「ボランティアはたいせつだと思うけど、勉強やアルバイトでいそがしくて、なかなか時間がとれない。」 What challenge does the writer describe?
options: Not being paid for the volunteer work they do
Not knowing where to find volunteer work nearby
Parents who will not let them do volunteer work
Finding time for it alongside study and part-time work
questions.explanation: The writer agrees volunteering matters (たいせつだと思う) but cannot easily find time (なかなか時間がとれない) because of study and part-time work. Pay, location and parents are not raised.

questions.stem: 「毎週、近所のおとしよりの家をたずねて、話しあいてになっています。」 What volunteer work does the speaker do?
options: Teaching older neighbours to use a phone each week
Doing the shopping for an older neighbour every week
Cleaning an older neighbour's house once a week
Visiting an older neighbour every week to keep them company
questions.explanation: 「たずねる」 is to visit and 「話しあいてになる」 is to be someone to talk with. The community benefit is company for older people who may live alone; shopping or cleaning are not mentioned.

questions.stem: 「スクーリーズでは、レッドフロッグスというグループのボランティアが、卒業生をあんぜんにホテルまでおくったり、朝ごはんにパンケーキを作ったりします。」 What do these volunteers do?
options: Clean the hotels and teach school leavers to cook pancakes
Walk school leavers safely back and cook them pancake breakfasts
Organise the parties and sell pancakes to the school leavers
Drive school leavers home and pay for their hotel breakfasts
questions.explanation: 「あんぜんにホテルまでおくる」 is to see someone safely back to their accommodation, and 「パンケーキを作る」 is to cook pancakes. The 「〜たり〜たり」 lists examples of their work.

questions.stem: 「さいがいのあと、ボランティアセンターが、だれがどこで何をするかを決めています。」 Why does the centre do this?
options: So that volunteers are paid fairly for the hours that they work
So that only trained professionals are allowed into the area
So that volunteers can choose freely where they would like to go
So that crowds of helpers are coordinated, not chaotic
questions.explanation: The centre decides who does what and where (決めています). When huge numbers of uncoordinated volunteers arrived after the 1995 earthquake, the result was confusion, which is why coordinating centres became standard.

questions.stem: 「みんなが少しずつ時間を出せば、町はもっときれいになります。」 What does the sentence say?
options: If everyone gives a little time, the town will become cleaner
Everyone gave a little time, so the town became cleaner
Even if everyone gives time, the town will not become cleaner
The town is cleaner when only a few people give their time
questions.explanation: 「出せば」 is the 「ば」 conditional of 「出す」: 'if everyone puts in'. 「もっときれいになります」 is the result. The sentence is a hypothetical, not a report of something done.

questions.stem: 「ボランティアをするなら、まず近くの公園のそうじから始めたらどう？」 What is the speaker suggesting?
options: If you're going to volunteer, start by cleaning your local park
Once you've cleaned the local park, you can stop volunteering
You should volunteer at the park instead of cleaning your room
If the park is clean, there is no need for volunteering
questions.explanation: 「〜なら」 picks up the listener's plan ('if you're going to volunteer'), and 「〜たらどう？」 makes a casual suggestion. 「まず〜から始める」 is to start with something.

questions.stem: Asked 「ボランティアは学校のじゅぎょうにするべきだと思いますか。」, which reply gives an opinion with a reason?
options: 「はい、私の学校にもボランティアクラブがあります。」
「ボランティアは毎年、十二月にあります。」
「先生もボランティアをしたことがあります。」
「いいえ、自分でえらんでするほうが、意味があると思います。」
questions.explanation: The question asks whether volunteering should be a school subject. Only the first reply states a view (いいえ) and backs it up: choosing for yourself is more meaningful (意味がある). The others give facts with no opinion.
